newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Koreans doubt Pyongyang's prophet of doom.
newsitem.headline: South Koreans doubt Pyongyang's prophet of doom.

text.p: He arrived in Seoul as a prophet of doom, a voice from Stalinist North Korea warning of missile attacks, chemical warfare and a nuclear "sea of fire".

But if defector Hwang Jang-yop -- the most senior North Korean ever to betray his homeland -- expected his cousins in the South would tremble at his predictions that the North was preparing war, he was mistaken.
Many people in South Korea, their suspicions honed by decades of Cold War propaganda, are wondering whether Hwang is really who he claims to be.
Some say he is a fake, a creation of the country's intelligence agencies playing a well-known political game of scare-mongering in an election year. Presidential polls are scheduled for December.
"There's something fishy about him," said Dae Suk, a buddhist monk.
"This seems to be another tactic used by the government during an election year to scare the public into voting for a ruling party candidate."
Jung Man-sung, 28, a computer programmer, was equally sceptical. "I don't believe Hwang's words," he said.

Since he arrived in April after fleeing via China and the Philippines, Hwang has been in the care of South Korea's Agency for National Security Planning. The U.S. Central Intelligence Agency has also had access to him.
Last week, at his first major news conference, he speculated about the origins of a war that he said was coming "sooner or later" on the instructions of Pyongyang leader Kim Jong-il.
Perhaps the North would catch South Korea off-guard at a time of social turmoil, Hwang mused. His suggestion: no more demonstrations or labour strikes.

Such advice echoes precisely the line taken over the years by hawks in the security services and the ruling camp, who have frequently invoked the North Korean threat as an excuse to crack down on students and the opposition.
"Hwang might be conveying a war mood created for political purposes. His comments lacked specifics and evidence," said Lee Jong-seok, a fellow at the Sejong Institute, a private think-tank.
Lee dismissed Hwang's arguments that the North would launch a war out of desperation, bravely flying the "red flag of revolution" to the dying end.
"You are talking about a you-die-and-I-die war. There is no such war in the history of mankind," he said.
Hwang conceded at his news conference he had no proof to back up his earlier assertion that North Korea could "scorch" South Korea, and even Japan, with nuclear arms.
Although U.S. officials have not said so openly, they privately concede that Hwang was not the prize catch they had hoped for.

As a Workers' Party theorist -- the architect of Pyongyang's "juche" ideology -- they point out that Hwang has limited credentials as a commentator on military affairs. Besides, since the 1950-53 Korean War ended in a truce, South Korea and its U.S. ally have been prepared for war at a moment's notice.

"No enlightening information emerged from his news conference," said Park Sung-hoon, a director-general at Seoul's National Unification Ministry. "North Korea's goal in the past 50 years has been taking the South by force."
"We have been trying to bring the North to a dialogue table. I see no shift in our policy."
Officials from the two Koreas, the United States and China are due to meet in New York on August 5 to prepare for four-way peace talks.
Hwang said North Korea had no intention of suing for peace, and was only interested in using its participation in the talks as leverage for more food aid.
Kim Hak-joon, politics professor at Inchon University, said Kim Jong-il's game was blackmail, not war.
"Kim Jong-il has displayed a tendency of sealing deals after securing benefits for his country by using blackmail as a major weapon in diplomacy and negotiations," he said.

Earlier threats to turn the South into a "sea of flames" resulted in a deal with Washington in 1994 under which North Korea is to receive safe nuclear reactors and interim fuel supplies worth $4.5 billion.
